questions.question: Define utility, distinguish value in use from value in exchange, and resolve the water-diamond paradox.
questions.expected_answer: Utility is the satisfaction or usefulness a consumer derives from a good — subjective, living in the user, varying by person, place and moment (the umbrella in the storm). Value in use is usefulness to the owner; value in exchange is what a thing fetches when traded, with price being exchange value expressed in money. The paradox: water (immense use-value) exchanges cheaply while diamonds (ornamental) exchange dearly, because exchange value is governed by scarcity relative to wants and the utility of the NEXT unit — water is abundant so another glass adds little; diamonds are rare. Plenty cheapens; scarcity dearens.

questions.question: List the perfect market's conditions and classify the three imperfect structures with examples and the price taker/maker distinction.
questions.expected_answer: Perfect market: many buyers and sellers (none able to influence price alone), homogeneous product, perfect knowledge, free entry and exit — every participant a price taker; fresh produce markets and the share market approximate it. Imperfect structures: monopoly — one seller, no substitutes (sole utility, patented medicine), a price maker; oligopoly — a few large sellers watching each other (banks, networks, fuel); monopolistic competition — many sellers of differentiated products (restaurants, salons), each with small pricing power. Classify by three questions: number of sellers, similarity of product, freedom of entry.

questions.question: Describe the effects of electronics on markets (both directions) and the five functions of markets.
questions.expected_answer: Electronics widened markets (global reach for local sellers), accelerated them (continuous trading, second-by-second prices), brightened knowledge (prices visible to anyone with a phone — the farmer negotiating from information), lowered entry barriers (selling without a shopfront) and created new forms (platforms, apps). Balanced against: platform-owner power, exposure to world competition, and the digital divide as a new barrier. The five functions: price formation through demand and supply; allocation — prices steer resources toward what society wants; information — prices as compressed messages; rationing — rising prices decide who receives scarce goods; linking buyers and sellers who never meet. Markets make prices, and prices do the rest — for those with buying power.
